bug-evolution.note: Suggested by an AI session from the model's description and the base records. No expert has checked these links yet.

anchors.label: Computer Models
anchors.why: Students watch natural selection happen in a population of individual beetles.

thinkingTools.label: Causal Mapping
thinkingTools.why: Students can map how speed, predators and survival depend on each other.

thinkingTools.label: Tinbergen's Questions
thinkingTools.why: The model keeps two questions apart, what speed is for and how the beetle population came to be fast.

concepts.label: Natural selection
concepts.why: Predators catch slower beetles more often, so faster beetles leave more offspring.

concepts.label: Adaptation
concepts.why: Running speed is a trait that helps beetles survive.

concepts.label: Selection pressure
concepts.why: Birds and spiders hunt in different ways, so they push beetle speed in different amounts.

concepts.label: Variation
concepts.why: Beetles in the population differ in how fast they run.

concepts.label: Agent-based modeling
concepts.why: Each beetle and each predator follows its own simple rules, and the population pattern comes out of that.

competencies.label: Explaining natural selection step by step
competencies.why: Students trace how differences, survival and inheritance together change a population.

competencies.label: Reasoning with models in evolution
competencies.why: Students use a computer model to test ideas and to see where the model is too simple.

theories.label: Restructuration (Wilensky and Papert)
theories.why: An idea that is hard as a population-level formula can be easier when students see individuals following rules.

theories.label: Individual-rules thinking may come first
theories.why: A claim in our theory work that this kind of model helps learners reach a full explanation of natural selection. The claim is still being tested.

literature.label: Wilensky and Papert (2010), Restructurations
literature.why: The idea behind building models of individuals to teach population-level ideas.

literature.label: Aslan and Wilensky (2016), Restructuration in practice
literature.why: Uses an agent-based model to take apart a popular misunderstanding of evolution.

literature.label: Goldstone and Wilensky (2008), Promoting transfer
literature.why: Evidence on how simulations help students carry a principle to new cases.

evolution-ethnocentrism.note: Suggested by an AI session from the model's description and the base records. No expert has checked these links yet.

anchors.label: Computer Models
anchors.why: Students watch ethnocentric behavior rise or fall in a population made of several ethnic groups.

anchors.label: Cultural Diversity
anchors.why: The model invites reflection on in-group favoritism across human groups, with care about what it can and cannot say.

anchors.label: Cooperation Games
anchors.why: Agents choose how often to help others in their own group and in other groups, and the model shows which choices spread.

thinkingTools.label: Causal Mapping
thinkingTools.why: A map shows how helping, group markers and reproduction depend on each other.

thinkingTools.label: Noticing Tool
thinkingTools.why: Students can notice their own reactions to the results and ask where those reactions come from.

concepts.label: Cooperation
concepts.why: Agents decide whether to help, and the model shows when each choice pays off.

concepts.label: Kin selection
concepts.why: Helping others who share your traits can spread those traits.

concepts.label: Frequency-dependent selection
concepts.why: How well a strategy does depends on how common it already is.

concepts.label: Selection at more than one level
concepts.why: Selection between individuals and between groups can pull in different directions.

concepts.label: Agent-based modeling
concepts.why: Each agent follows simple rules about whom to help, and the group pattern comes out of those rules.

competencies.label: Reasoning about selection at several levels
competencies.why: Students weigh what helps an individual against what helps its group.

competencies.label: Working across cultures
competencies.why: The follow-up discussion connects the model to how people treat those outside their own group.

theories.label: Group markers and cooperation
theories.why: Shared markers such as a color or a symbol can let cooperation reach beyond people who know each other, which is also how the model's agents tell who is in their group.

theories.label: Restructuration (Wilensky and Papert)
theories.why: An idea that is hard to grasp in the abstract can be easier when students see individuals following rules.

literature.label: Richerson and others (2016), Cultural group selection and cooperation
literature.why: Evidence that selection between groups helps explain human cooperation.

literature.label: Mesoudi (2011), Cultural evolution
literature.why: A book-length account of how culture changes by selection and copying.

teachingbase.label: Cognitive biases, ethnocentrism and the blind spot
teachingbase.why: A related lesson on how in-group bias shapes what people notice.

evolution-resource-use-social-behavior.note: Suggested by an AI session from the model's description and the base records. No expert has checked these links yet.

anchors.label: Computer Models
anchors.why: Students watch harvest behavior and punishment evolve in a population over many generations.

anchors.label: Governing the Commons
anchors.why: Monitoring and punishing greedy harvesters is one way real groups protect a shared resource.

thinkingTools.label: Causal Mapping
thinkingTools.why: A map shows how harvesting, punishment, resource stock and reproduction loop back on each other.

concepts.label: Cooperation
concepts.why: Sustainable harvesters help the whole group, and punishers help keep it that way.

concepts.label: Tragedy of the commons
concepts.why: Greedy harvesters can use up the resource unless something holds them back.

concepts.label: Selection at more than one level
concepts.why: Greedy harvesters do better inside a group while groups with sustainable harvesters last longer.

concepts.label: Group selection
concepts.why: Groups that keep their resource going can outlast groups that do not.

concepts.label: Agent-based modeling
concepts.why: Each agent follows its own harvest and punishment rules, and the group pattern comes out of those rules.

competencies.label: Reasoning about selection at several levels
competencies.why: Students weigh what helps an individual against what helps its group.

competencies.label: Reasoning with models in evolution
competencies.why: Students use a computer model to test ideas and to see where the model is too simple.

theories.label: The commons dilemma
theories.why: The standard account of why shared resources get overused and what changes the outcome.

theories.label: Design principles for cooperating groups
theories.why: Monitoring and graduated sanctions are among the conditions that help groups manage a shared resource.

theories.label: Individual-rules thinking may come first
theories.why: A claim in our theory work that this kind of model helps learners explain cooperation and social dilemmas. The claim is still being tested.

literature.label: Ostrom (1990), Governing the commons
literature.why: Shows how real communities monitor and sanction to keep shared resources going.

literature.label: Wilson, Ostrom and Cox (2013), Core design principles
literature.why: Sets out the design principles behind groups that cooperate well.

literature.label: Hardin (1968), The tragedy of the commons
literature.why: The classic statement of the problem the model shows.

anchors.label: Computer Models
anchors.why: Students vary the mix of modest and greedy foresters and watch what happens to each community.

anchors.label: Governing the Commons
anchors.why: Two communities draw on one regrowing forest, so the group's rules and mix of people matter.

thinkingTools.label: Payoff Matrices
thinkingTools.why: Students can tabulate the short-term gain and long-term cost of modest and greedy harvesting.

thinkingTools.label: Causal Mapping
thinkingTools.why: A map shows how the mix of foresters, harvest and tree regrowth depend on each other.

concepts.label: Social dilemma
concepts.why: Individual short-term gain pulls against the community's long-term welfare.

concepts.label: Tragedy of the commons
concepts.why: Enough greedy foresters can use up the forest for everyone.

concepts.label: Social-ecological system
concepts.why: The communities and the forest form one connected system.

concepts.label: Cooperation
concepts.why: Communities with more modest foresters keep the forest and their harvest for longer.

concepts.label: Agent-based modeling
concepts.why: Each forester follows a simple harvest rule, and the community results come out of those rules.

competencies.label: Working together toward shared goals
competencies.why: Students test what it takes for groups to keep a shared resource going.

competencies.label: Systems thinking
competencies.why: Students follow how individual choices add up to community and forest outcomes.

theories.label: The commons dilemma
theories.why: The standard account of why shared resources get overused and what changes the outcome.

theories.label: Design principles for cooperating groups
theories.why: A set of conditions that help groups manage a shared resource, which students can compare with what they see in the model.

theories.label: Individual-rules thinking may come first
theories.why: A claim in our theory work that this kind of model helps learners explain cooperation and social dilemmas. The claim is still being tested.

literature.label: Hardin (1968), The tragedy of the commons
literature.why: The classic statement of the problem the model shows.

literature.label: Ostrom (1990), Governing the commons
literature.why: Shows how real communities keep shared resources going.

literature.label: Basurto and Ostrom (2009), Beyond the tragedy of the commons
literature.why: Argues that outcomes depend on how a community is set up, which the two-community mix lets students explore.

literature.label: Wilson, Ostrom and Cox (2013), Core design principles
literature.why: Sets out the design principles behind groups that cooperate well.

anchors.label: Computer Models
anchors.why: A small system with two people and one forest that students can run again and again.

anchors.label: Governing the Commons
anchors.why: Two people share a resource that regrows, which is the smallest version of a commons.

anchors.label: Cooperation Games
anchors.why: Each forester's best choice depends on what the other forester does.

thinkingTools.label: Payoff Matrices
thinkingTools.why: Students can tabulate what each forester gains for each pair of choices.

thinkingTools.label: Causal Mapping
thinkingTools.why: Harvest, regrowth and the stock of trees feed back on each other, and a map shows the loop.

thinkingTools.label: Analogy Mapping
thinkingTools.why: Students can compare the forest with a fishery, a well or the climate.

concepts.label: Social dilemma
concepts.why: What is best for one forester in the short run can leave both worse off.

concepts.label: Tragedy of the commons
concepts.why: Greedy harvesting can use up a shared resource faster than it regrows.

concepts.label: Social-ecological system
concepts.why: The forest and the foresters' choices form one connected system.

concepts.label: Cooperation
concepts.why: Both foresters do better when each takes a modest share.

concepts.label: Agent-based modeling
concepts.why: Each forester follows a simple harvest rule, and the outcome comes from how the rules meet.

competencies.label: Working together toward shared goals
competencies.why: Students test what it takes for two parties to keep a shared resource going.

competencies.label: Systems thinking
competencies.why: Students follow how harvest, regrowth and the stock of trees affect each other over time.

theories.label: The commons dilemma
theories.why: The standard account of why shared resources get overused and what changes the outcome.

theories.label: Interests that partly line up and partly clash
theories.why: The dilemma appears when individual and shared interests are neither the same nor opposite, as with the two foresters.

theories.label: Individual-rules thinking may come first
theories.why: A claim in our theory work that this kind of model helps learners explain cooperation and social dilemmas. The claim is still being tested.

theories.label: Restructuration (Wilensky and Papert)
theories.why: An idea that is hard to grasp in the abstract can be easier when students see individuals following rules.

literature.label: Hardin (1968), The tragedy of the commons
literature.why: The classic statement of the problem the model shows.

literature.label: Ostrom (1990), Governing the commons
literature.why: Shows how real communities keep shared resources going.

literature.label: Goldstone and Wilensky (2008), Promoting transfer
literature.why: Evidence on how simulations help students carry a principle to new cases.
